## Proof

Let $n = 2566$ and define
$$P(x) = \prod_{k=1}^{n}(kx+1).$$

**Key observation.** Differentiating $P(x)$ using the product rule gives
$$P'(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} j\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n}(kx+1).$$

Factoring out $P(x)$ from each term (i.e., writing $\prod_{k\neq j}(kx+1) = \frac{P(x)}{jx+1}$), we obtain
$$P'(x) = P(x)\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{j}{jx+1}.$$

This is precisely the integrand. Therefore
$$\int_0^1 \prod_{k=1}^{n}(kx+1)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{j}{jx+1}\right)dx = \int_0^1 P'(x)\,dx = P(1)-P(0).$$

**Evaluating the endpoints.**

$$P(0) = \prod_{k=1}^{n}(0+1) = 1,$$

$$P(1) = \prod_{k=1}^{n}(k+1) = 2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdots (n+1) = (n+1)! = 2567!.$$

**Conclusion.**

$$\int_0^1 \prod_{k=1}^{2566}(kx+1)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{2566}\frac{j}{jx+1}\right)dx = 2567! - 1.$$
